items.why: A fully realized tree has no wings, so nothing is lacking in this one.

items.text: A human being who cannot see
items.why: Blindness is the absence of sight in a thing whose nature calls for sight. Notice it is an absence, not an added thing.

items.text: A human being who cannot see infrared light
items.why: No human sees infrared. This is not a failure to be what a human being is.

items.text: A dog that cannot do algebra
items.why: Dogs are not rational animals. Nothing proper to a dog is missing here.

items.text: A dog born with a malformed leg
items.why: Four working legs belong to what a dog is. This dog falls short of its own kind.

items.text: A desire for money, taken on its own
items.why: Wanting money is not bad in itself. In a murder for money, what is bad is the missing intention to seek it justly.

items.text: The ache you feel the day after a hard workout
items.why: Pain is not bad as such — it flags danger and damage. This one isn't even experienced as bad.

items.text: A sadist's pleasure at another's suffering
items.why: Desire aimed away from the concern for others that social animals need: a deformity of soul, as blindness is of the eye.

ch6b.title: From a tree's inclination to the will of God
ch6b.caption: Will is rational appetite — inclination toward what one grasps as worth pursuing. Feser climbs from plants to God, then argues that at the top it is free.
ch6b.where: Will: from natural inclination to the divine will (pp. 223–224)

nodes.text: A tree inclines to sink roots, with no awareness at all
A dog consciously seeks food and water: sensory appetite
We incline to what we grasp as worth pursuing: will
nodes.note: Rational appetite. We can conceptualize what we are after, and so pursue or refuse it for reasons.

nodes.text: So there is in God something answering to what we call will
Though he need do nothing to realize his nature
nodes.note: He is not like something that never inclined at all, but like something whose realization is already complete. Call it the limit case of rational appetite.

nodes.text: He grasps every possible thing, and wills some of them to be
nodes.note: Lion and unicorn are both concepts in the divine intellect. One was willed into existence; the other was not.

nodes.text: Nothing outside him could compel him — all else depends on him
Nothing inside him necessitates: unicorns were as possible as lions
So the divine will is free
nodes.note: Easier to state negatively — nothing compels him, within or without — than to picture positively. Our own freedom is famously hard to picture too.

ch6b.title: Known truly, never comprehended fully
ch6b.caption: Feser's position is neither 'we can say nothing' nor 'we have God figured out'. Both halves of this table are consequences of the same arguments.
ch6b.where: Incomprehensibility: known truly, never comprehended fully (pp. 229–232)

columns.label: What we really do know
columns.sub: and it is genuine knowledge
items: That he exists, and why — by arguments you can check
What he is not: not composite, not changeable, not in time
Positive attributes said analogically: power, knowledge, goodness
That God is to his goodness as a tree is to its goodness

columns.label: What we cannot do
columns.sub: and the limit is principled, not lazy
items: Break him into parts and see how they fit — he has none
Name his genus and specific difference — he falls under none
Keep a firm grip as the creaturely limits get stripped away
Expect better: this is the deepest level of reality there is

ch6b.note: The paradox is only apparent: God is hard to understand precisely because he is simple — 'simple' here meaning without parts, not easy. And this is what any attempt at ultimate explanation should look like. Physics also ends up saying strange things once it leaves the everyday world where our words were learned.

ch6b.title: Why the world would blink out
ch6b.caption: Divine conservation: creation is not something that happened once. It is happening now, and nothing in the world has the resources to keep itself going.
ch6b.where: Conservation: creation at every moment, no existential inertia, no pantheism (pp. 232–234)

links.text: This chair exists right now
links.note: Not: it was made in a factory once. What makes it be, at this instant?

links.text: …but it is a mixture of actuality and potentiality
links.note: And its essence — what a chair is — is one thing; its existing is another.

links.text: …so something must be actualizing its existence, now
…and nothing composite can do that for itself
links.note: Parts are only potentially combined until something combines them. Whatever does the combining cannot be one of the parts.

links.text: God, holding it in being at this very instant
links.note: And he is not the world: the world is composite, changing and contingent; he is simple, immutable and necessary. So this is not pantheism — nor panentheism, which would have the world changing him.

ch6b.collapse: Withdraw the bottom member and the world does not wind down or decay. It is simply not there, at that instant. That is what conservation means — and it is why 'existential inertia' has nothing to coast on.

ch6b.title: Occasionalism, concurrentism, mere conservationism
ch6b.caption: Does the sun really melt the ice? Three answers, and why Feser takes the middle one. The same principle — action follows being — rules out both extremes.
ch6b.where: Concurrence: between occasionalism and mere conservationism (pp. 234–238)

columns.label: Occasionalism
columns.sub: only God ever causes anything
items: The sun does not melt the ice; God does, when the sun is out
The cue ball does not move the eight ball; God does
Created things have no causal power, not even derived

columns.label: Concurrentism
columns.sub: real causes, none of them independent
items: The sun really melts the ice — and cannot do it without God
Like blue chalk: it makes the square blue, you make there be a square
Like the moon: the light is really its own, and all of it received

columns.label: Mere conservationism
columns.sub: God keeps things going, then stands back
items: God keeps the sun in being; the sun melts the ice on its own
Causal power owned outright rather than on loan
Tidier — and in effect a form of deism

ch6b.note: Occasionalism fails because action follows being: what truly does nothing would not truly exist — and you know at least that you exist, and that you are not God. Mere conservationism fails by the same principle run the other way: what could act independently of God could exist independently of him, which the proofs rule out. Both are like climbing a ladder carefully and then blasting it out from under you.

ch6b.title: What a miracle actually is
ch6b.caption: Drop Hume's definition and the standard 'miracles are incoherent' argument has nothing to attack. Feser's alternative: beyond nature, never against it.
ch6b.where: Miracles I: why “violation of a law of nature” is the wrong definition (pp. 238–241)

nodes.text: Hume's definition: a miracle is a violation of a law of nature
nodes.note: On which the sceptic's argument writes itself — evidence of a violation would just be evidence the 'law' was never a law.

nodes.text: But a law describes how a thing tends to act, given its nature
nodes.note: The laws of nature are the laws of natures. Water freezes at 32 °F because of what water is.

nodes.text: A tendency can be blocked, or its trigger absent, with no breach
nodes.note: Supercooled liquid water below freezing breaks no law; the disposition is there and simply does not manifest.

nodes.text: And if laws follow natures, they cannot be violated at all
nodes.note: Anything that reliably turned to mousse at 32 °F would not have been water in the first place.

nodes.text: So a miracle is not below nature but beyond it
nodes.note: A defect is sub-natural. A miracle is super-natural: nature raised to a power its own nature cannot account for. Only God can cause one.

nodes.text: Some miracles add: the loaves and fishes, a resurrection
Some subtract: the furnace that does not burn
nodes.note: Not God forcing fire to act against its nature. He refrains from conserving and concurring, so the normal effect never arrives — a suspension of the law, not a breach of it.

nodes.text: And never an intervention: he is no cause alongside causes
nodes.note: You cannot intervene in what you are doing yourself. Not a machinist tinkering with a faulty machine, but a musician improvising on a score he is already playing.

ch6b.title: Objection anatomy: the paradox of the stone
ch6b.caption: The classic schoolyard version of the problem of omnipotence. It dissolves once you ask whether the phrase describes anything.
ch6b.says: Can God make a stone too heavy for him to lift? If he can, there's something he can't do — lift it. If he can't, there's something he can't do — make it. Either way, something is beyond him, so he isn't omnipotent.
assumes: That 'a stone too heavy for God to lift' names a possible thing
That failing to do anything we can describe is always a lack of power
ch6b.breaks: The description is self-contradictory, exactly like 'round square'. A stone's rising is something that could occur, so it is something God can cause — for any stone whatever. So there is no such object as a stone he could not lift, and therefore no such power as the power to make one.
ch6b.reply: Your question has the same shape as 'can God draw a square circle?' Stringing words together doesn't automatically name a task. Since a stone's rising is possible, God can make any stone rise — so 'a stone God can't lift' describes nothing at all. He isn't failing at it; there's no it. The same goes for sinning: a perfectly good being that sins is a contradiction, not a feat he's too weak for.

ch6b.title: Objection anatomy: foreknowledge and free will
ch6b.caption: Two confusions bundled into one objection — one about knowing, one about causing. Feser's author analogy handles the second.
ch6b.where: Infallible foreknowledge rules out free will
ch6b.says: If God infallibly knows I'll go to work tomorrow, then I can't do otherwise — otherwise he'd have been wrong, and he can't be wrong. So the choice isn't free. And it's worse than that: he's the cause of tomorrow, so he's making me do it.
assumes: That someone's knowing what you do has some grip on your doing it
That God's causing you is like one thing inside the world pushing another
ch6b.breaks: Knowing is not making. My knowing you are sitting in the next room, however certain I am, does nothing to your having freely sat there — and moving my knowledge to the future changes nothing about that. As for causing: God is not a cause among causes. He is not a character in the story; he is its author.
ch6b.reply: Suppose I watch you on a live feed and see you take the chocolate. My certainty didn't reach in and choose for you. Now shift my knowledge a day earlier — it still doesn't touch your choosing. And on causing: a novelist can write a story in which a character freely plots a murder, and nobody says 'he only did it because the author wrote it that way.' You would say that about a hypnotist inside the story, interfering with another character. The author is not a character at all.

ch6b.title: Objection anatomy: must evil be in God?
ch6b.caption: The objection turns Feser's own principle against him. The answer is what kind of thing badness is — and this is how the problem of evil is handled in this chapter.
ch6b.where: By proportionate causality, evil must be in God
ch6b.says: You've insisted a cause must contain whatever is in its effects. The world is full of evil. So by your own principle, evil is in God — which is the opposite of what you want to conclude.
assumes: That evil is a positive item in the world, like heat or mass
That anything we can name about an effect must be in the cause
ch6b.breaks: The principle is about what is there — positive features. Badness is a privation: the absence of a good that a thing of that kind should have had. So making a world with evil in it is not making two sorts of stuff. It is making good things while refraining from making some of the good that could have been there.
ch6b.reply: Proportionate causality says what is in the effect is in the cause. Evil isn't in the effect in that sense — it is precisely what isn't there. I draw two sides of a triangle and stop: the defect isn't an extra thing I put in, it's what I left out. And leaving it out needn't be a defect in me — I might be using the unfinished triangle to teach something. Courage cannot exist unless people face real danger; a world containing that good must carry that badness too.

ch6b.title: Objection anatomy: existential inertia
ch6b.caption: The most serious naturalist reply to conservation. Feser's answer has two halves: nobody says what the feature is, and nothing composite could have it.
ch6b.where: Existential inertia: things might just keep existing
ch6b.says: Why think anything needs holding in being? Once a thing exists it presumably just keeps existing under its own steam until something destroys it — the way a moving body keeps moving. Conservation is an extra assumption doing no work.
assumes: That continuing to exist needs no more explaining than continuing to move
That some contingent thing could have this feature without our being told what gives it
ch6b.breaks: Two problems. Its proponents never say what it is about a material object that could confer such a remarkable power. And nothing composite could have it in any case: whatever is a mixture of act and potency, or has an essence distinct from its existence, is merely potential until something actualizes it — now, not once upon a time.
ch6b.reply: Tell me what in the chair confers that power. It's a mixture of what it is and what it could be, and being a chair isn't the same as existing — so at this instant something has to be making it be rather than not be. 'It just keeps going' isn't an answer to that argument; it's a decision not to engage with it. The same reply blocks 'maybe the world itself is the necessary being': the world is composite, changing and contingent, and nothing like that can be necessary.

ch6b.title: Objection anatomy: can an unchanging God love?
ch6b.caption: It feels like the strongest objection in the chapter, because it appeals to something we all recognize. The reply asks what love essentially is.
ch6b.says: To love is to be moved by the one you love — a parent's worry when the child is in distress, a lover who can't stop thinking about her. Being moved is being changed. So an unchanging God is emotionally inert, and cannot love anyone.
assumes: That love essentially consists in feelings the beloved produces in you
That because our loving involves being affected, all loving must
ch6b.breaks: A fallacy of accident again. What is essential to love is willing what is good for the beloved. That is exactly why we call love shallow when it consists only of feelings that wax and wane, and why tough love and love of enemies count as love at all. Love belongs to the will, which is active, not to the emotions, which are passive.
ch6b.reply: Ask what makes love serious rather than sentimental: willing the other's good even on the days you don't feel it. That's the core; the feelings are what it's like in creatures who have nervous systems. God wills things into existence, and to create a tree is to will that it have what is good for a tree — roots, water, light. That is loving it, in the most active sense there is.

ch7a.title: The argument nobody defended
ch7a.caption: Most published 'refutations' target a three-line summary that no major defender of the cosmological argument ever put forward. Compare it with the real thing.
ch7a.where: The straw man: the “basic cosmological argument”

columns.label: The 'basic cosmological argument'
columns.sub: as textbooks and critics present it
items: Anything that exists has a cause of its existence
Nothing can cause its own existence
The universe exists
So the universe has a cause outside it

columns.label: What defenders actually argue
columns.sub: Aristotle to Aquinas to Leibniz
items: Whatever goes from potential to actual has an actualizer
Whatever is composite needs its parts held together
Whatever has essence distinct from existence needs it imparted
Start from any one thing — no premise about the universe needed

ch7a.note: Even the critic who framed the 'basic' version conceded that no one has defended an argument of that form, calling it a useful stepping stone. Feser's complaint: it is a stepping stone to a false impression, since the real arguments never said everything has a cause, never assumed a beginning, and mostly never reason about the universe as a whole at all.

ch7a.title: Where the confusion started: two senses of 'cause'
ch7a.caption: Clarke's diagnosis of how the Hume-Russell tradition got going. Descartes and Spinoza used one word for two different things, and the objection has been recycled ever since.
ch7a.where: Where the confusion began: two senses of “cause”

columns.label: Cause, efficient sense
columns.sub: something that actualizes a potential
items: Always distinct from its effect
Nothing can be its own efficient cause
The sense in which God is said to have no cause
This is the sense the objection needs to work

columns.label: Cause, sufficient-reason sense
columns.sub: whatever makes something intelligible
items: May lie in the thing's own nature
So something can be self-explanatory, if not self-caused
Descartes and Spinoza meant something like this
In this sense everything has one — God included

ch7a.note: Hume read the rationalists' 'everything has a cause' in the first sense when they meant something closer to the second — and from there the misreading became a tradition, repeated by critics who cite other critics rather than the defenders themselves.

ch7a.title: Drill: could this be where the series stops?
ch7a.caption: Everyone agrees something has to be at the bottom. The test is whether the candidate has any potentiality, any parts, or an essence distinct from its existence.
ch7a.where: “Maybe the universe (or Big Bang, multiverse, quantum events, laws of physics) is the uncaused cause”
ch7a.prompt: Could this be the uncaused terminus of the series?

items.text: The universe as a whole
items.why: It changes constantly, so it is riddled with potentiality, and it is composite through and through.

items.text: The Big Bang
items.why: An event, and one located in time. The proofs are not about what started things off in the first place.

items.text: A beginningless multiverse
items.why: Adding more universes adds more composite, changing things. The series gets longer, not deeper.

items.text: The quantum vacuum
items.why: Empty space with energy in it, governed by laws — not nothing, and shot through with states it could be in but isn't.

items.text: The fundamental laws of physics
items.why: A law is shorthand for how a thing of a certain nature behaves. It needs things with natures, and the question is why there are any.

items.text: Fundamental particles
items.why: They have distinct attributes, and they come into being and pass away. Both mark potentiality.

items.text: Conserved mass-energy
items.why: It takes different forms at different times — which is to say it is potentially otherwise than it is.

items.text: The number 7
items.why: Abstract objects are causally inert. Seven has never made anything happen.

items.text: Something purely actual, with no unrealized potential at all
items.why: Nothing in it could need actualizing, so it not only has no cause but could not have had one. The Aristotelian proof's terminus.

items.text: Something absolutely simple, with no parts of any kind
items.why: No parts means nothing needing to be combined, and so nothing for a cause to have done. The Neo-Platonic proof's terminus.

items.text: Something whose essence just is its existence
items.why: Nothing has to join what it is to that it is, so its existing was never something to be imparted. The Thomistic proof's terminus.

ch7a.title: Objection anatomy: a universe from nothing
ch7a.caption: The popular-science version of the argument's defeat. It turns on a word that quietly changes meaning between the title and the body.
ch7a.where: “Physics shows the universe can arise from nothing”
ch7a.says: Physics has shown how a universe can come from nothing. Because there is a law like gravity, the universe can and will create itself out of nothing. So we no longer need any metaphysical cause of the world.
assumes: That 'nothing' names some especially thin kind of stuff that physics might study
That a law of nature is available before there is anything for it to be a law of
ch7a.breaks: A law like gravity is not nothing. Neither is empty space with energy in it, nor a quantum field, nor layers of physical law. Nothing is the absence of anything at all — it is not a candidate for empirical study and nothing follows from it. Whatever these accounts start from is a something, and every such something is composite and potential.
ch7a.reply: Ask what the 'nothing' is. In the books that promise it, it turns out to be empty space with energy, or a quantum field, or a law of gravity — and the authors admit as much before the end. That is not nothing; it is a very interesting something, and exactly the kind of something the argument asks about. And nothing isn't a strange, hard-to-measure substance. It is the absence of anything whatever.

ch7a.title: Objection anatomy: 'even so, why call it God?'
ch7a.caption: Treated by many critics as the knockdown reply. Feser's response is simply that the arguments for the attributes exist, run to hundreds of pages, and go unanswered.
ch7a.where: “Even if there were a first cause, there’s no reason to think it would be God”
ch7a.says: Suppose you get to a first cause. There is absolutely no reason to think it is omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good, or personal. Getting from an uncaused cause to the God of traditional religion is the usual big jump.
assumes: That defenders stop at 'a first cause' and then simply assert the rest
That no arguments from first cause to the divine attributes have been given
ch7a.breaks: The claim is not that the jump is invalid but that no one bridged it — and that is simply false as a matter of record. Aquinas devotes roughly a hundred dense pages of the Summa Theologiae to it right after the Five Ways, and hundreds more elsewhere; Clarke's book is largely about the attributes; this book's Stage 2 sections and the whole of chapter 6 do the same.
ch7a.reply: There's no jump; there's an argument, and it takes chapters. From pure actuality you get immutability, and from immutability eternity, and from that immateriality — and unity, and power, and intellect. You may think one of those steps fails. Say which. What you can't say is that no reason has been offered, because the reasons fill more pages than the existence proofs do.

ch7b.title: Scientism, and the four problems with it
ch7b.caption: Most modern objections to natural theology rest on an unstated premise: that only science delivers knowledge. Feser attacks the premise itself.
ch7b.where: Scientism: the hidden premise and its four problems

nodes.text: The hidden premise: only science gives us real knowledge
nodes.note: Rarely argued for. It is usually doing its work in the background of 'that's not science, so it doesn't count'.

nodes.text: Problem 1: that claim is not itself a result of any experiment
nodes.note: So by its own standard it is not knowledge. It is a philosophical thesis about the limits of knowledge.

nodes.text: Widen 'science' to cover it, and the claim goes trivial
nodes.note: If science means any careful, evidence-sensitive reasoning, then metaphysics is science too, and the objection has lost its bite.

nodes.text: Problem 2: physics keeps only what can be mathematicized
nodes.note: It abstracts from everything else by design. That is why it is so precise — and why its silence about something is not evidence of absence.

nodes.text: Problem 3: laws of nature cannot be the final explanation
nodes.note: A law is shorthand for how a thing of a certain nature behaves. So laws presuppose things with natures; they cannot account for there being any.

nodes.text: Problem 4: from predictive success to completeness is a non sequitur
nodes.note: Metal detectors are superbly good at finding metal. That tells you nothing about whether there is wood and stone.

ch7b.title: Defense and theodicy — two different jobs
ch7b.caption: Knowing which question is on the table settles most confusion about the problem of evil. Feser only needs the first one for his purposes.
ch7b.where: The problem of evil (I): defense versus theodicy, and Mackie’s logical argument

columns.label: A defense
columns.sub: is evil consistent with God existing?
items: Answers the atheist's claim of outright contradiction
Needs only to show how both could be true together
Does not have to say why any actual evil is permitted
Enough to rebut the objection — this is Feser's focus

columns.label: A theodicy
columns.sub: why does God permit the evils there are?
items: A far more ambitious project
Would name the reason for this suffering, in this life
You can succeed at the first without attempting this
Not required to answer the argument from evil

ch7b.note: Mackie's logical argument was that omnipotence plus perfect goodness plus evil is a contradiction. He later conceded that it is not — that evil does not show the central doctrines of theism to be logically inconsistent. That concession is a defense succeeding, whatever remains open about theodicy.

ch7b.title: Objection anatomy: who designed the designer?
ch7b.caption: Dawkins's central argument, aimed squarely at design arguments — which is why it sails past the five proofs without touching them.
ch7b.where: Who designed the designer? A designer is even more complex
ch7b.says: Anything capable of designing a universe would have to be at least as complex as the universe itself, and complex things need explaining. So the designer hypothesis multiplies what needs explaining. A simpler explanation is more probable.
assumes: That the argument being attacked reasons from complexity to a designer
That it is a probabilistic inference, so a rival could be more parsimonious
That God is being proposed as a complex thing
ch7b.breaks: It is aimed at Paley-style design arguments, and none of the five proofs is one. They never appeal to complexity, never reason from analogy with human artifacts, never weigh probabilities — a pebble or a drop of water serves the Neo-Platonic proof as well as an eye does. And they entirely agree with the objection's principle: anything composite needs a cause, which is precisely why they conclude to something with no parts at all.
ch7b.reply: You and I agree completely: a complex cause would need a cause of its own. That's my premise, not my problem. That is exactly why the argument doesn't stop at anything composite — it goes all the way to something absolutely simple. And this isn't a probability comparison, so 'a simpler hypothesis is more likely' doesn't engage it. It claims to be a demonstration. Find the false premise.

ch7b.title: Objection anatomy: 'go one god further'
ch7b.caption: A slogan that assumes the God of classical theism is one item on a list with Zeus and Thor. Feser answers with two analogies from outside religion.
ch7b.says: You already disbelieve in Zeus, Odin, Thor, Quetzalcoatl and thousands of others. I just go one god further. You're being selective in your scepticism; I'm being consistent.
assumes: That the God of classical theism belongs to the same class as Zeus and Thor
That disbelieving in members of that class extends naturally to him
ch7b.breaks: A category mistake. Zeus and Odin are beings within the world — powerful, composite, changeable, located. The God argued for here is not a member of that class at all; he is subsistent existence itself, the reason anything in any class exists. Extending disbelief from one to the other is not consistency; it is a change of subject.
ch7b.reply: Imagine someone saying: Euclideans already agree that the triangles drawn in books have imperfectly straight sides — I just go one triangle further and say triangularity itself has crooked sides. That's confused, because triangularity isn't one more drawn triangle. Same here. Classical theism's God isn't the best-behaved member of the pantheon. If atheism were true it wouldn't be because he turned out to be one more absent Thor.

ch7b.title: Objection anatomy: evil disproves God
ch7b.caption: Mackie's version, in which evil and God are strictly inconsistent. Two words in his second premise do all the damage.
ch7b.where: Evil proves God doesn’t exist (the logical problem)
ch7b.says: God is supposed to be omnipotent and perfectly good. There are no limits to what an omnipotent being can do, and a good being eliminates evil as far as it can. Evil exists. So either God isn't omnipotent, or isn't good, or isn't there.
assumes: That omnipotence means there is literally nothing an omnipotent being cannot do
That a good being always eliminates every evil it is able to eliminate
ch7b.breaks: Both halves of the second premise fail. Even omnipotence does not extend to contradictions, so if some goods logically require certain evils, not even God could have the goods without the evils. And a good agent does not always remove every evil it can: a good parent does not spare the child the unpleasantness of homework, because removing it would remove the learning.
ch7b.reply: Take forgiveness. It cannot exist unless someone has actually done something wrong. Take courage — it needs real danger. Take compassion — it needs someone who has genuinely suffered. God could have made a world with free will and no evil in it; what he could not have made is a world with free will, no evil, and all the moral good this one contains. That's not a limit on his power any more than not making round squares is.
